It's worth starting by noting that Europe isn't a single country, but many countries, and each of them has different traditions with respect to immigration. Further, most Europeans, if you track our ancestry back far enough, are immigrants. There are many French with British ancestry, or German, or Italian; there are many Brits with French ancestry, German, or Italian. Migration within Europe has been common for centuries. In addition, many Europeans have historically been hospitable to migrants from non-European countries. There's been a Chinatown in London for longer than the United States has even existed, there were North Africans in the north of England two thousand years ago and Arab traders one thousand years ago, France has gladly welcomed Turks, Africans and native South Americans for centuries, and further east there has been a constant interplay between Europe and Asia. There are many things that divide Europeans, but (although there have been many regrettable incidents to the contrary) the entire continental culture has been moving towards openness and acceptance of diversity. The most international city on the planet is London, and this internationality is a large part of the reason why London is so successful.

Your suggestion that adding new people "dilutes" the original culture is false, because it assumes that culture is static. In fact, the only static cultures are dead cultures. Each new layer of immigrants may change a culture, but the culture remains. Take food as an example: English culture now includes the balti, German culture now includes the döner kebab (which Wikipedia says is as popular in Germany as burgers or sausages), and Romanian cuisine has taken the best of Ottoman and Arab recipes for centuries. Europeans are proud of their ability to grow and learn from every new immigrant. The remark that European cultures are being "swamped" misunderstands how migration works: most people who move to Europe are moving for a better life, and quickly adopt many aspects of the local culture they migrate to. Cultures are not swamped, they are absorbed. In my personal acquaintance are an English boy whose family roots are in Pakistan whose only dream is to play for Arsenal; a Frenchman whose family roots are in China, but who is typically Parisian in every aspect of his personality; a Pole whose roots are in Nigeria, but is as devout and proud a Polish catholic family man as anyone else in Poznań; and many more. Immigrants form less than 4% of the European population; this isn't "swamping".

So, that's a bit about Europe's history, and how immigration really works - first generation immigrants may retain their original cultures to some extent, but a generation or two later the natural human desire to fit in has eroded this away. So let's focus on the benefits of immigration. Of these, the most important is purely economic: economies that are open to migration tend, over time, to do better than those that restrict migration. Further, what really benefits a country isn't a selective immigration policy: inviting a few PhDs into a country might give a short-term and local boost, but what really matters is an open-door policy. This is because if you open the economy to wide immigration it turns out that the immigrants you get are (by and large) people who are hard-working, ambitious, and don't mind taking the less glamorous jobs. These people pay their taxes, by and large don't claim excessive benefits from the state (tabloid scare stories make headlines because cases where immigrants are exploiting the social security system are rare, not because they're common), and, best of all, produce a next generation who are pushed to work hard at school, get into university, and excel. Children in immigrant families face pressure because "we moved to Europe to give you children a better life, so don't let us down". Wide immigration produces the next generation's middle classes and professionals - accountants, doctors, engineers, scientists.

Immigration has the additional advantage for many European countries of providing support for a declining population: in many European countries the non-immigrant birth rate is below the population replacement rate, so it's useful to bring in new people to maintain the existing level of economic activity. Immigration does bring its problems, but the evidence of much research over many years is that the benefits outweigh the costs; that's why Europe should welcome new Europeans.
